justification_text:
The consistent point estimate of 61.56 across all time horizons – one day, one week, and one month – indicates that this value likely represents either the current observed state of the variable or a very stable historical average. My forecast assumes that, in the absence of specific new information or expected drivers for change, the metric is most likely to remain at or revert to this baseline. This approach suggests a belief in the inherent stability of the variable over the short-to-medium term, implying that no significant upward or downward trend is currently anticipated within these horizons.

The varying widths of the 90% confidence intervals reflect the natural increase in uncertainty as the forecast horizon extends. For the one-day outlook, the narrow interval [60.36, 62.76] shows high confidence in the immediate future, largely influenced by the current stability and recent historical fluctuations. As we look further out to one week [58.85, 64.27] and especially to one month [56.13, 66.99], the intervals broaden significantly. This widening accounts for the greater potential for random variability, the accumulation of small, unpredictable influences over time, and the general decrease in predictive power inherent in longer timeframes.

While the forecast provides a central estimate and a range of likely outcomes, certain unforeseen events or systemic shifts could push the actual results beyond these stated intervals. Such risks could include sudden, unexpected policy changes, significant economic shocks, major geopolitical developments, or even technological breakthroughs or failures that fundamentally alter the underlying conditions influencing the metric. These types of "black swan" events or rapid, large-scale changes are difficult to quantify in probabilistic forecasts and represent the primary risks for outcomes falling outside the projected 90% confidence bands.
